issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette:
For thirty-eight years, Michael had walked into spaces that could kill him. As a bomb disposal technician, he had learned to read a room the way a musician reads a score—every wire, every shadow, every faint chemical tang in the air was a note that could signal the end of the piece. But the day that ended his career was not a bomb. It was a sealed storage container in a decommissioned military depot, a job he had done a hundred times before, and the slow, invisible leak from a corroded cylinder that released a cloud of methyl isocyanate into his face before his respirator was fully sealed. He felt the burn in his throat and eyes within seconds, and by the time his team pulled him out, his lungs were already seizing. He spent eleven days in the intensive care unit, tethered to oxygen, the antiseptic smell of the hospital seeping into his dreams. He was discharged with a clean bill of physical health, but something in his mind had not been discharged at all.

In the months that followed, Michael found himself unable to step into his own garage without his heart hammering. The garage smelled faintly of cleaning solvents, and the association was immediate and visceral—his mouth would go dry, his hands would tremble, and he would be back in that container, gasping. He began to avoid the garage entirely, then the basement, then any room in his house that was not the living room or the kitchen. Being alone in a room felt like being trapped in that container again; he needed to know that someone else was nearby, that if something happened, there would be a witness, a rescuer. His wife, Grace, noticed that he would follow her from room to room, and when she asked why, he said he just liked being near her. But the truth was that he was terrified of the silence of an empty space.

His work became his refuge. Michael requested every overtime shift he could get, and his supervisors praised his dedication. But the truth was that when he was working—sweeping a field for ordnance, checking a suspicious package—his mind had no room for the memory of the container. The moment he stopped, the moment he sat down in a quiet break room, the smell of antiseptic would creep into his nostrils, and his chest would tighten. So he kept moving. He worked twelve-hour days, then fourteen. He volunteered for the most remote assignments. He came home exhausted, fell into bed, and woke up to do it again. Grace began to complain that she never saw him, that he was always at work, but Michael could not explain that staying home meant staying alone with the thought that he was going to die, that his lungs would collapse again, that nobody would find him in time.

Everywhere he went, his eyes moved before his feet did. He could not enter a restaurant without scanning for the exits. He could not sit in a waiting room without noting which door led outside, whether it was unlocked, whether there was a window he could break. He had always been vigilant on the job, but now vigilance had become a constant, exhausting companion. When someone touched his shoulder unexpectedly—a colleague, a cashier, even Grace in bed—he would flinch violently, his arm shooting out as if to ward off an attack. He knew it was irrational, but in that split second, his body was certain that the touch was the start of something that would suffocate him.

It was a routine physical examination that finally broke the pattern. His doctor, a well-meaning young woman, pressed a stethoscope to his chest, and Michael felt his vision narrow. The smell of the exam room—alcohol wipes, latex gloves, the faint chemical undertone of sterilized instruments—flooded his senses. He stood up abruptly, knocking over a tray of instruments, and walked out without a word. He sat in his car in the parking lot, shaking, and realized that he could not go back. He could not face another examination, another ambulance siren on the street, another hospital corridor. He had not been to a doctor since his discharge, and now he understood why: the medical world itself had become a trigger.

Grace found him in the car an hour later. She sat beside him and said, quietly, that she had been reading about what he was going through. She said she thought he needed to talk to someone. Michael did not answer. He stared at the hospital building in the rearview mirror and felt the familiar urge to drive away, to find another shift, to bury the memory under more work. But he was sixty-two years old, and he was tired. He was tired of scanning every room, of flinching at every touch, of being unable to sit still in his own home. He was afraid that if he stopped, the memory would finally catch up to him. But he was also afraid that if he did not stop, he would lose Grace, and his health, and whatever was left of a life that was not defined by a single, invisible moment of poison in the air. So he nodded, and he let her make the appointment, and he sat in the waiting room with his back to the wall, watching the door.
